what_it_does: The self-attention operation at the heart of every transformer-based language model has many variants — causal masking, sliding windows, positional biases, document boundaries, paged memory layouts, and more. Each variant historically required a separate hand-tuned GPU program (called a kernel), creating a maintenance nightmare and blocking researchers from trying new ideas. FlexAttention is a programming interface in PyTorch that lets a user describe any attention variant in a few lines of ordinary Python, then compiles it into a single high-performance GPU kernel that matches or exceeds the speed of those hand-written programs.
method_in_detail:
The idea. FlashAttention, the standard high-performance attention implementation, works by never materializing the large intermediate score matrix in GPU global memory (high-bandwidth memory chips). Instead it computes attention in small tiles that fit in the GPU's fast on-chip memory (SRAM), keeping a running numerically stable maximum so the normalization step — softmax, which turns raw scores into probabilities that sum to one — can be computed tile by tile without seeing all scores first. This tiled approach makes attention fast and memory-efficient but is compiled as a fixed program; supporting a new masking pattern or scoring rule traditionally requires rewriting the entire kernel.

FlexAttention's interface. The user writes two small Python functions. 'score_mod' takes a raw attention score and the positions of the query and key tokens and returns a modified score — for example, adding a distance penalty for the ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases) positional encoding scheme. 'mask_mod' takes the same positions and returns true or false — for example, 'return q_position >= k_position' for a causal mask that prevents a token from attending to future tokens. These functions are captured by PyTorch's compiler (torch.compile) and translated into small Triton code blocks (Triton is a GPU programming language). Those blocks are then inserted into a hand-written attention kernel template that already implements all the FlashAttention tile-level optimizations.

Block-level sparsity. A naive approach would apply mask_mod to every individual score scalar at runtime, adding overhead even for fully masked tiles. FlexAttention pre-computes a compact BlockMask: it divides the score matrix into blocks (128 tokens x 128 tokens by default) and categorizes each block as fully unmasked (skip the mask entirely), partially masked (apply mask_mod element by element), or fully masked (skip the block completely, saving 100% of its compute). This precomputed structure fits in a small index array, not in the huge full score matrix. The GPU kernel uses the block index to jump directly to the next non-masked block, hiding memory latency by prefetching the next block's keys and values while computing the current one.

Paged memory. For inference serving, models store their running notes (key-value records for past tokens) in non-contiguous physical memory pages rather than one contiguous array, to avoid wasted space between requests of different lengths. FlexAttention reuses the BlockMask index as a page table, transparently translating logical token positions to physical memory locations inside the same indirect memory access path, adding less than 1% overhead.

The result. Across seven attention variants, FlexAttention achieves 0.68x-1.43x the speed of hand-optimized FlashAttention-v2 for training and 0.93x-1.45x for inference decoding — competitive on all supported variants and the only option for unsupported ones. End-to-end it speeds up LLaMA fine-tuning by 2.4x and LLaMA inference serving by up to 2.04x compared to PyTorch's default attention implementation.
